reference.one_line: 72-year-old woman with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer and complete malignant bowel obstruction, comfort-focused, symptoms controlled on PCA and nasogastric suction; hospice house transfer 18 Nov 11:00.

handoff.summary: Platinum-resistant ovarian cancer with complete multilevel small bowel obstruction; no surgical or venting option. Comfort-focused since 16 Nov: No CPR, no intubation, no blood tests. Pain 3/10 and nausea 1/10 on hydromorphone PCA 0.3 mg/h (8.4 mg in the last 24 hours), octreotide, dexamethasone and haloperidol; nasogastric output about 90 to 100 mL per 4 hours. Alert and peaceful. Alderbrook Hospice House has accepted her; ambulance tomorrow at 11:00.
to_do: Get metoclopramide stopped before the 18:00 dose: palliative care advised this on 15 Nov and cramps follow every dose
Have pharmacy or palliative care re-check the transfer morphine before the pump is loaded at about 10:00: 168 mg in 24 h is the oral equivalent; subcutaneous is about 56 mg (2.3 mg/h)
Octreotide 15:00 and 23:00, haloperidol 21:00; pump check every 4 hours; mouth care every 2 hours
Transfer summary, medication reconciliation, signed resuscitation form in the envelope; code status line in today's note corrected
if_then: If her heart or breathing stops, then no CPR and no intubation: comfort measures, call son Emrys (proxy) and the team
If pain is above 5/10 or she needs more than 3 boluses in 4 hours, then call palliative care to adjust the PCA
If sudden severe constant abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen, then suspect perforation: treat symptoms, call the team and family; no imaging without discussion

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mrs Skelhorne-Ibekwe, 72, with stage IIIC high-grade serous ovarian cancer, platinum-resistant and progressing through gemcitabine (last dose 20 Oct), was admitted on 14 Nov after three days of vomiting with no stool or flatus since 11 Nov. CT showed complete small bowel obstruction with at least three transition points from peritoneal carcinomatosis, without ischaemia or perforation. A nasogastric tube drained 1,400 mL in the first hour. Dehydration and kidney injury improved with fluids (creatinine 1.5 to 1.1 mg/dL). General surgery advised against operation and interventional radiology found no safe window for a venting gastrostomy. With palliative care, symptoms were controlled on a hydromorphone PCA (0.3 mg/h continuous; 8.4 mg used in the last 24 hours), octreotide, dexamethasone and haloperidol; nasogastric output fell from 1,180 mL on 15 Nov to 760 mL on 16 Nov. Palliative care also advised stopping metoclopramide; it remains active and cramping follows each dose. At a family meeting on 16 Nov she chose comfort-focused care with no CPR, no intubation, no further blood tests and no heparin. Alderbrook Hospice House accepted her for 18 Nov with the nasogastric tube on portable suction and a subcutaneous morphine infusion, the dose of which must be re-checked before the pump is loaded.

problem_list.problem: Complete malignant small bowel obstruction at multiple levels, no surgical or venting option
High-grade serous ovarian cancer, platinum-resistant, with progressing peritoneal carcinomatosis and ascites
Cancer pain on long-term opioids, now hydromorphone PCA
Low potassium, contraction alkalosis and kidney injury from vomiting
Malnutrition, albumin 2.3 g/dL, 9 kg lost in 6 months
Comfort-focused care; No CPR, no intubation; hospice transfer

reconciled_medications.medicine: Hydromorphone PCA 0.3 mg/h with 0.2 mg bolus
reconciled_medications.reason: Hospice pumps use morphine; 8.4 mg in 24 h is about 56 mg subcutaneous morphine.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Morphine 168 mg over 24 hours (7 mg/h) subcutaneous, to start at transfer
reconciled_medications.reason: Three times too high: 168 mg is the oral equivalent. About 2.3 mg/h with a breakthrough dose; double-check still outstanding.
Complete obstruction; palliative care said stop on 15 Nov; colic after each dose; duplicates haloperidol.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Octreotide 200 micrograms every 8 hours; haloperidol 1 mg every 8 hours; dexamethasone 8 mg daily
reconciled_medications.reason: Controlling secretions and nausea; review dexamethasone after 5 days.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Pantoprazole 40 mg daily; lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed
reconciled_medications.reason: Home medicines, now intravenous; hospice to choose the route.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Lactated Ringer's 40 mL/h; artificial saliva spray
reconciled_medications.reason: Comfort; hospice will decide about fluids.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Morphine extended-release 60 mg twice daily; morphine 15 mg as needed
reconciled_medications.reason: No oral route; replaced by the infusion.

reconciled_medications.medicine: Senna 17.2 mg nightly; polyethylene glycol 17 g daily; ondansetron 8 mg as needed
reconciled_medications.reason: Complete obstruction and no oral route; palliative care: no laxatives.

pending_items: Double-check of the hydromorphone to morphine conversion (requested by the hospice nurse, not done)
Medication reconciliation, transfer summary and prescriptions
Ambulance 18 Nov 11:00; PCA to stop and pump to be loaded at about 10:00

qa.q: Where is the bowel obstructed on CT?
qa.a: At least three transition points: mid jejunum, distal ileum, and a pelvic loop encased by a 6.2 cm deposit. No ischaemia or perforation.

qa.q: What are the current PCA settings?
qa.a: Hydromorphone 0.2 mg/mL: 0.3 mg/h continuous, 0.2 mg bolus, 10-minute lockout.

qa.q: Who is her health care proxy?

qa.a: Per shift: 660 and 520 mL on 15 Nov, 430 and 330 mL on 16 Nov, 200 mL so far today; per 4 hours it fell from 260 to 90 mL.

qa.q: Did kidney function and potassium recover with fluids?
qa.a: Creatinine fell from 1.5 to 1.2 to 1.1 mg/dL. Potassium rose from 3.1 to 3.4, then was 3.3 mmol/L, still low when tests stopped.

qa.q: How did the tumour marker and albumin change from 28 Oct to admission?
qa.a: CA-125 rose from 1,120 to 1,840 U/mL; albumin fell from 2.9 to 2.3 g/dL.

qa.q: How long was the chart still full code after she signed the form?
qa.a: About three hours: she signed at 14:45 on 16 Nov, the order was entered at 17:50 and the wristband changed at 18:05.

qa.q: When do her cramps occur in relation to medicines?
qa.a: 20 to 30 minutes after each metoclopramide dose, for example doses at 00:10 and 06:10 with cramps at 00:35 and 06:35.

qa.q: Why can she not have a venting gastrostomy?
qa.a: An omental deposit lies over the front of the stomach and there is moderate ascites, so there is no safe window; she declined drainage of ascites for that purpose.

qa.q: Using the ratio in the palliative consult, what subcutaneous morphine dose equals her 24-hour hydromorphone use?
qa.a: 8.4 mg hydromorphone is about 56 mg morphine in 24 hours (2.3 mg/h). The 168 mg ordered is the oral equivalent, three times too much.

qa.q: Why a hospice house and not home hospice?
qa.a: The nasogastric tube and suction need nursing day and night and she does not want her son to carry that.

qa.q: What octreotide dose was she on before palliative care increased it?
qa.a: The chart does not say. The consult says increase to 200 micrograms, but no earlier octreotide order is recorded.

qa.q: Has the morphine conversion been double-checked?
qa.a: No check is documented. At 12:40 it was noted as not yet done and nothing later records it.

tasks.prompt: Review the active scheduled medicines for any that conflict with her diagnosis or with consult recommendations.
expected_findings: Metoclopramide 10 mg every 6 hours is still active, next dose 18:00
CT shows complete obstruction and the palliative consult of 15 Nov said to stop it (colic, perforation risk)
Flowsheet and night note show cramps 20 to 30 minutes after each dose
It duplicates dopamine blockade with scheduled haloperidol
acceptable_actions: Withhold the 18:00 dose and ask the team to discontinue metoclopramide
Continue haloperidol and octreotide; keep it off the transfer list

tasks.prompt: Verify the opioid conversion ordered for tomorrow's transfer.
expected_findings: The resident multiplied 8.4 mg intravenous hydromorphone by 20, which gives the oral morphine equivalent (168 mg), and ordered it subcutaneously at 7 mg/h
By the consult's ratio (1.5 mg hydromorphone = 10 mg parenteral morphine) the dose is about 56 mg in 24 h, 2.3 mg/h
The order is about three times too high; the hospice nurse's double-check has not been done
acceptable_actions: Correct the order to about 56 mg in 24 h (2.3 mg/h), or 25 to 50% less for the opioid switch, with a subcutaneous breakthrough dose
Have pharmacy or palliative care verify before the pump is loaded
must_not: Cut the dose so far that she is left in pain

tasks.prompt: Confirm the patient's resuscitation status across the orders and today's notes.
expected_findings: Today's progress note opens 'Code status: full code (to be readdressed at family meeting)', copied from the 16 Nov attending note
The active order, signed form and wristband say No CPR, no intubation
acceptable_actions: Treat her as No CPR, no intubation
Ask the resident to correct the note by addendum before the transfer summary
must_not: Reopen the decision with the patient because of the note

tasks.prompt: Determine when the patient made her decision about resuscitation and whether the chart reflected it promptly.
expected_findings: She stated the decision at 14:40 and signed the form at 14:45 on 16 Nov
The order was not entered until 17:50, about three hours during which the chart said full code
On 15 Nov she voiced the same wish but asked for no change, so that is not the decision time
acceptable_actions: Record 16 Nov 14:40 to 14:45 as the decision time
Raise the order-entry delay for review
must_not: Give 17:50 or 15 Nov as the time of decision

tasks.prompt: Assess whether the bowel regimen is appropriate for a patient on a continuous opioid.
expected_findings: No laxative is ordered and home senna and polyethylene glycol are on hold
This is deliberate: complete obstruction, no oral route, and palliative care says no laxatives and no stimulant laxative
acceptable_actions: Leave laxatives on hold and document the reason
must_not: Flag the missing laxative as an error
Order senna, bisacodyl or an enema

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Metoclopramide was not stopped that day: the 18:00, midnight and 06:00 doses were given and each was followed by cramping and extra PCA boluses. At 08:40 on 18 Nov the hospice nurse declined to load the pump until the conversion was checked; the palliative care physician confirmed that 168 mg was the oral equivalent, rewrote the infusion as subcutaneous morphine 55 mg over 24 hours with 5 mg breakthrough doses, stopped metoclopramide and had the code status line corrected. She left for Alderbrook Hospice House at 12:40, later than planned, with her son. The colic settled within a day. Fluids were stopped at her request on 21 Nov. She grew sleepier from 25 Nov and died peacefully on 29 Nov with both children present, eleven days after transfer.

events.event: Metoclopramide given (again at 00:10 and 06:10); cramping from 18:30 for 25 minutes, two PCA boluses
Palliative care checks conversion: morphine corrected to 55 mg in 24 h (2.3 mg/h) with 5 mg breakthrough; metoclopramide stopped
PCA stopped, subcutaneous morphine pump started by hospice nurse
Transferred by ambulance to Alderbrook Hospice House with son
Intravenous fluids stopped at her request; nasogastric suction continued
Morphine increased to 70 mg in 24 h; drowsy most of the day
Died at the hospice house, son and daughter present

outcomes_30_day.notable: Died 29 Nov at the hospice house, comfortable; the morphine error was caught before the pump was loaded.

portal_messages.subject: Palliative care referral
portal_messages.body: Dr Vantongeren mentioned a palliative care referral yesterday and I said I wanted to think. I have thought. Does seeing them mean you are finished with me? I am not ready to stop everything. But the pain tablets are not lasting until the next one and I am awake at night. Can they just help with the pain, or is it all or nothing?
ideal_reply_points: Palliative care works alongside oncology; it can be for pain alone
Ask how many breakthrough doses she takes

portal_messages.subject: Feeling sick, bowels slowing
portal_messages.body: I have felt sick for four days and am only passing small amounts. My tummy is tighter than usual. I had the blockage in September and do not want that again. Should I double the senna and take more of the powder, or do I need to come in? I have not actually been sick yet.
ideal_reply_points: Telephone her the same day; ask about vomiting, wind, pain and swelling
With a previous obstruction, do not escalate stimulant laxatives without assessment
Vomiting or no wind means the emergency department

portal_messages.subject: Tomorrow's move
portal_messages.body: This is Emrys, Philippa's son and health care proxy. Two things before tomorrow. The nurse said Mum's pain button comes off and she goes on a morphine pump. Her allergy list says codeine made her sick, so is morphine safe? And she had cramps again after six tonight, the same as every evening. Is that the cancer, or something we can fix before she is in an ambulance? I will be there from eight.
ideal_reply_points: Morphine is safe: she took it at home; codeine caused sickness, not allergy
The pump dose is being double-checked before loading
The cramps follow metoclopramide doses; it should be stopped

portal_messages.subject: Re: Tomorrow's move
portal_messages.body: Dear Emrys, morphine is safe for her: she took it by mouth at home for months, and the codeine problem was sickness, not an allergy. I am seeing her at half past eight to check the pump dose myself before anything is loaded. You are right about the cramps. They follow one of her anti-sickness injections, which I advised stopping; I will stop it this morning.

portal_messages.subject: Thank you, and a question
portal_messages.body: I am Tamsin, Philippa's daughter, writing from Lisbon. Thank you all. The last days at Alderbrook were gentle and she was herself almost to the end. A question I could not ask at the time: Mum's mother had breast cancer and Mum had ovarian. Was Mum ever tested for the gene, and should I be? I do not know who to ask here.
ideal_reply_points: Germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing in 2024 found no harmful variant
That lowers but does not exclude inherited risk; offer a summary for her own doctor

conversation.setting: Family meeting, 7 South quiet room, 16 Nov 14:00; nurse and chaplain also present

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: Thank you all for coming. Tamsin, I know you only landed this morning. Philippa, I'd like to say plainly where things stand, then hear from you. All right?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Plainly, please. I've had enough of people being careful.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: The scan shows the bowel is blocked by the cancer, and not in one place, in several. That's why nothing goes through and why the tube in your nose is doing the work.

turns.speaker: Tamsin
turns.text: Can't they operate? Cut the blocked bit out?

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: The surgeons looked carefully. With blockages at several levels there'd be disease above and below any join. It wouldn't be safe and it wouldn't work.

turns.speaker: Emrys
turns.text: And the drainage tube into the stomach they talked about on Sunday?

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: The radiologists went through the scan last night. There's a thick layer of cancer over the front of the stomach, and fluid. No safe way in.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: And more chemotherapy would be...

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: I don't have a treatment left that is likely to help you. I'm sorry. Nobody can be exact, but my honest answer on time is probably short weeks.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Weeks. Well. I thought as much.

turns.speaker: Dr. Fontaine-Okoro
turns.text: Philippa, yesterday you told me what you would and wouldn't want, and asked me to wait until both children were here. They're here. Would you like to say it yourself?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. I've thought about it since Saturday. If my heart stops, or my breathing, I don't want anyone pressing on my chest. No shocks. No breathing machine. Let me go quietly.

turns.speaker: Dr. Fontaine-Okoro
turns.text: I want to be sure I've understood. If your heart or breathing stopped, we'd keep you comfortable and not try to restart them. Everything for comfort carries on: the pain pump, the sickness medicine, the nurses. Is that what you mean?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's exactly what I mean.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: Emrys, Tamsin, how does that sit with you?

turns.speaker: Emrys
turns.text: It's what she's always said. I'm with her.

turns.speaker: Tamsin
turns.text: I don't like it. But it's hers to decide. Yes. I support it.

turns.speaker: Dr. Fontaine-Okoro
turns.text: Then there's a form, Philippa. You sign, and your nurse and I witness it. It goes with you wherever you go.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Give me the pen. And while we're at it: no more blood tests. And those injections in my tummy for clots, I don't want those either.

turns.speaker: Dr. Vantongeren
turns.text: That's reasonable, we'll stop both. I'm sorry, I'm being called to clinic. The resident will put the order in.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: Mrs Skelhorne-Ibekwe, where would you want to be? Home with nurses visiting, or a hospice house?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Not home. This tube needs someone night and day and I won't have Emrys doing it. A hospice house. I just want to be comfortable.

turns.speaker: Social worker
turns.text: I'll contact Alderbrook Hospice House today.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Good. Then it's settled. Is the chaplain still here? I'd like him to stay a while.

turns.speaker: Emrys
turns.text: I'll go and find him, Mum.
